title: The alert nobody had
outcome: Partitions ran on one copy for nine days without anyone knowing, until the last copy's broker failed.

content.bookmark: UnderReplicatedPartitions should be 0. A value above zero that lasts means the cluster is running with fewer copies than you think.

check.prompt: What is the normal value of the broker metric UnderReplicatedPartitions?
check.why: In a healthy cluster every partition has its full set of in-sync replicas. Non-zero means some followers have fallen out of the ISR.

check.prompt: How many brokers should report ActiveControllerCount = 1?
check.why: One active controller at a time. Zero or more than one is a problem to investigate.

check.prompt: Which two consumer signals do the Kafka docs say to watch?
options: Max lag below a threshold, and minimum fetch rate above zero
check.why: Lag shows falling behind; a fetch rate of zero shows a consumer that has stopped fetching altogether.

check.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 1 (the default). Two followers drop out of the ISR. Are acks=all writes accepted?
options: Yes, with only the leader holding them
check.why: acks=all waits for the current ISR, here just the leader, and min ISR 1 allows it. Writes succeed with one copy.

caseStudy.setting: An insurer (fictional) runs a 5-broker Kafka cluster for claims processing. Monitoring was set up quickly at launch: consumer lag dashboards and broker CPU. Topics use replication factor 3 and the default min.insync.replicas of 1.

events.what: A broker's network card starts dropping packets. Its followers can't keep up, and after replica.lag.time.max.ms the leaders remove it from the ISR of many partitions. A second broker is under maintenance and down.
Producers and consumers work normally. Lag is fine. Nobody looks at replication.
The broker leading many of those partitions fails. With no in-sync replica left, the partitions go offline. Claims processing stops.

tasks: Which metric would have shown the problem on day 1?
Why did writes keep succeeding with one copy?

debrief.title: The signal that was there
text: UnderReplicatedPartitions went above zero on day 1 and stayed there. IsrShrinksPerSec spiked too. Both are standard broker metrics with a normal value of 0.
Nobody alerted on them. Lag and CPU looked healthy, because producers and consumers were unaffected while one copy remained.

debrief.title: Why writes kept working
text: acks=all waits for the current in-sync replicas, not all assigned ones. With the ISR shrunk to the leader, acks=all was satisfied by one broker.
min.insync.replicas of 1 allowed it. At 2, writes would have been refused on day 1, which is disruptive but loud. UnderMinIsrPartitionCount would have shown it.

debrief.title: What happened on day 9
text: With every in-sync replica gone, Kafka by default waits for one to return rather than electing an out-of-sync replica (unclean.leader.election.enable=false). The partitions were unavailable rather than wrong.
The minimum alert set: UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0, UnderMinIsrPartitionCount > 0, ActiveControllerCount, UncleanLeaderElectionsPerSec, and consumer max lag and minimum fetch rate.

takeaway: Healthy clients can hide an unhealthy cluster.
Alert on under-replicated and under-min-ISR partitions, not just lag.
min ISR 2 turns silent risk into a loud error.
content.honesty: If you haven't set up Kafka monitoring, say so and name the metrics you'd alert on and why. If you have, lead with the alert that mattered most.

tasks: What would you ask about monitoring before launch?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "How would we know if we were one failure away from losing data?"

debrief.title: Requirements
text: Alerts on reduced redundancy, with an owner and a response time, tested before launch.

sayIt.question: What would you expect monitoring to cover before a Kafka-based service goes live?
points: Client health: consumer lag and that consumers are fetching.
Cluster health: under-replicated and under-min-ISR partitions, exactly one active controller.
Business health: events flowing at the expected rate.
An owner and response time for each alert.
A test that the alerts fire.

tasks: What do you tell claims handlers and customers?
How do you treat operational work in the roadmap?

debrief.title: Communication
text: Tell handlers claims are paused and when they resume; check whether any customer deadline was missed.

debrief.title: Roadmap
text: Monitoring done quickly at launch was never revisited. Schedule operational readiness as roadmap work with acceptance criteria.

sayIt.question: An outage happened because a warning went unnoticed for days. What do you change?
points: Communicate impact and recovery time.
Own that monitoring was incomplete.
Put operational readiness on the roadmap, not as leftover work.
Agree alert ownership.
Review monitoring after every incident.

tasks: What becomes part of operational readiness?

debrief.title: Recovery
text: Bring back a broker that held the data, let replicas catch up and rejoin the ISR, confirm UnderReplicatedPartitions returns to 0.

debrief.title: Operational readiness
text: A standard alert set for every cluster, tested; a weekly review of cluster health metrics.

sayIt.question: How would you set up operational readiness for a Kafka platform?
points: A standard set of cluster and client alerts.
Named on-call owners with response times.
Alert tests and runbooks.
Regular review of health metrics, not just incidents.
Maintenance procedures that check redundancy first.

tasks: Which alerts and thresholds would you set?
Which topic settings would you change?

debrief.title: Alerts
text: UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0 for a few minutes; UnderMinIsrPartitionCount > 0 immediately; ActiveControllerCount sum ≠ 1; IsrShrinksPerSec sustained; consumer records-lag-max above threshold and fetch rate at 0.

debrief.title: Settings
text: min.insync.replicas=2 on claims topics, so a shrinking ISR stops writes instead of silently reducing copies.

sayIt.question: Which Kafka metrics would you alert on, and why?
points: UnderReplicatedPartitions: should be 0; above means fewer copies.
UnderMinIsrPartitionCount: writes with acks=all are being refused.
ActiveControllerCount: exactly one across the cluster.
Consumer max lag and minimum fetch rate.
Request latency and handler idle time for capacity.
